more_info.banned_in:
Approved in the EU.
FDA lists turmeric oleoresin under 21 CFR 73.615; coverage of the purified E100 curcumin preparation was not verified in 2026.
more_info.overview: Curcumin is the principal yellow pigment in turmeric. Food-grade E100 is a concentrated extract containing curcumin and related pigments. It adds yellow to orange colour to foods.
more_info.origin: Plant-derived. Ground turmeric rhizomes are extracted with solvents, and the extract is crystallised to concentrate the colouring compounds.
more_info.daily_intake: 0–3 mg/kg body weight per day (JECFA, 2004); 3 mg/kg body weight per day (EFSA, 2010).
more_info.side_effects:
At food-use exposures, EFSA retained its ADI; its 2014 assessment nevertheless estimated that some high-consuming toddlers and children could reach or exceed it. These are exposure estimates, not observed symptoms.
At high experimental doses, reduced weight gain in second-generation rats was the endpoint used to set the ADI. This animal evidence does not establish the same effect at ordinary human food intakes.
more_info.uses: Examples of permitted EU uses include certain processed cheeses, spreads, fruit preparations and processed potato products. The categories and limits depend on the food.
more_info.dietary_restrictions: The pigment is extracted from turmeric, a plant, so the pigment itself is compatible with vegan and vegetarian diets.

more_info.banned_in:
Approved in the US.
INS 100(ii) identifies turmeric; the EU database lists E100 as curcumin, so a separate EU colour approval for turmeric powder was not verified in 2026.
more_info.overview: Turmeric is the ground rhizome of Curcuma longa. It provides yellow to orange colour and flavour. The INS entry for turmeric powder is distinct from the concentrated curcumin colour.
more_info.origin: Plant-derived. The colour material described by FDA is made by grinding turmeric rhizomes.
more_info.daily_intake: No ADI allocated for turmeric (JECFA, 1986). JECFA noted that turmeric is often treated as a food rather than a food additive.
more_info.uses: Used as a spice in foods such as curries and mustard. FDA permits turmeric as a colour in foods generally, subject to standards of identity and good manufacturing practice.
more_info.dietary_restrictions: Ground turmeric is a plant ingredient and is compatible with vegan and vegetarian diets.

more_info.banned_in:
Approved in the EU.
Approved in the US.
more_info.overview: Riboflavin is vitamin B2 and a yellow food colour. It occurs naturally in foods and can also be added as a nutrient. Its colour use is covered by E101(i) in the EU specifications.
more_info.daily_intake: 0–0.5 mg/kg body weight per day, as a group ADI with riboflavin-5'-phosphate (JECFA, 1981). EFSA did not allocate an ADI in 2013 because the long-term toxicology data were insufficient.
more_info.side_effects:
At authorised food-use levels, EFSA found no safety concern in 2013.
For high combined intakes, evidence was insufficient to assess adverse effects.
more_info.uses: Added as a yellow colour to foods. Examples in the EU database include certain fruit preparations and processed potato products; US colour use is subject to good manufacturing practice.

more_info.banned_in:
Approved in the EU.
Approved in the US.
The US listing covers nutrient use under 21 CFR 184.1697; it does not establish a colour-additive listing (checked in 2026).
more_info.overview: Riboflavin-5'-phosphate sodium is a phosphate derivative of vitamin B2. It provides yellow colour under the EU E101(ii) specification. FDA also lists it as a nutrient ingredient, which is a different permitted function from colouring.
more_info.origin: Made by chemically phosphorylating riboflavin. The sodium salt is supplied in a hydrated form; the FDA provision lists several phosphorylation reagents.
more_info.daily_intake: 0–0.5 mg/kg body weight per day, expressed as riboflavin, as a group ADI with riboflavin (JECFA, 1981). EFSA did not allocate an ADI in 2013 because of gaps in long-term toxicology data.
more_info.side_effects:
At authorised food-use levels, EFSA found no safety concern in 2013.
For high combined intakes, evidence was insufficient to assess adverse effects.
more_info.uses: A yellow food colour in the EU riboflavin group. In the US, 21 CFR 184.1697 covers nutrient supplementation of milk products and use in infant formula under the applicable conditions.

more_info.banned_in:
Approved in the EU.
Approved in the US.
more_info.overview: Tartrazine is a manufactured azo dye that gives food a yellow colour. It is sold in the US as FD&C Yellow No. 5. Food-grade material is a purified salt mixture meeting colour specifications.
more_info.origin: Synthetic. An aromatic sulfonic acid is diazotised, coupled to a pyrazole compound, and the dye is purified as its sodium salt.
more_info.daily_intake: 0–10 mg/kg body weight per day (JECFA, 2016). EFSA retained 7.5 mg/kg body weight per day in 2009; these are distinct assessments.
more_info.side_effects:
At food-use levels, EFSA reported intolerance reactions in a small fraction of people; reactions can occur within the ADI. Studies of colour mixtures with sodium benzoate do not establish that tartrazine alone causes behavioural changes.
At high experimental doses, reduced body weight in rats was the endpoint for JECFA's 2016 ADI. This animal evidence does not establish the same effect at food-use levels in humans.
more_info.uses: Examples include certain flavoured processed cheeses, processed peas and fish products. Other permitted uses depend on the food category; US batches require FDA certification.
more_info.precautions: EFSA noted that sensitive individuals may react at intakes within the ADI.

more_info.banned_in: JECFA records withdrawn specifications in 1984; this is not a national ban.
more_info.overview: Alkannin is a red-brown pigment found in plants including dyer's alkanet. Its historical food-colour identity is INS 103. A numbering-system entry does not establish current food-use approval.
more_info.origin: Plant-derived. The natural dye is obtained by extracting dyer's alkanet, Alkanna tinctoria.

more_info.banned_in:
Approved in the EU.
EU permitted levels and categories were reduced from 2013; no US food-colour listing was verified in 2026.
more_info.overview: Quinoline Yellow WS is a yellow food dye based on sulfonated quinophthalone compounds. It is a mixture of colouring salts rather than a single pure molecule. Its role in food is to supply yellow colour.
more_info.origin: Synthetic. A quinolyl indandione starting material is sulfonated to make the dye mixture, mainly supplied as sodium salts.
more_info.daily_intake: 0.5 mg/kg body weight per day (EFSA, 2009). JECFA established 0–3 mg/kg body weight per day in 2016; the two bodies' values differ.
more_info.side_effects:
At food-use levels, EFSA could not firmly attribute reported intolerance reactions to this dye because the evidence was limited. Its 2015 assessment estimated exposure below the ADI after EU use limits were reduced.
High-dose animal toxicity studies supplied the basis for the ADIs. They do not demonstrate comparable effects at normal human food intakes.
more_info.uses: Examples of permitted EU categories include confectionery, flavoured drinks, desserts and some sauces, with category-specific limits.

more_info.banned_in: JECFA records withdrawn specifications in 1984; no current EU or US food-colour listing was verified in 2026.
more_info.overview: Fast Yellow AB is a monoazo colour also identified as C.I. Food Yellow 2. Its historical food-colouring role is to supply yellow colour. JECFA identifies it under the former E105 number.
more_info.daily_intake: ADI decision postponed (JECFA, 1977). This is not an ADI stated as unspecified.

more_info.banned_in:
Approved in the EU.
Approved in the US.
E106 is retained as the repository identifier; the matching EU specification is E101(ii), not a separate E106 approval (checked in 2026).
more_info.overview: Riboflavin-5'-phosphate sodium is a phosphate derivative of vitamin B2. It provides yellow colour under the EU E101(ii) specification. FDA also lists it as a nutrient ingredient, which is a different permitted function from colouring.
more_info.origin: Made by chemically phosphorylating riboflavin. The sodium salt is supplied in a hydrated form; the FDA provision lists several phosphorylation reagents.
more_info.daily_intake: 0–0.5 mg/kg body weight per day, expressed as riboflavin, as a group ADI with riboflavin (JECFA, 1981). EFSA did not allocate an ADI in 2013 because of gaps in long-term toxicology data.
more_info.side_effects:
At authorised food-use levels, EFSA found no safety concern in 2013.
For high combined intakes, evidence was insufficient to assess adverse effects.
more_info.uses: A yellow food colour in the EU riboflavin group. In the US, 21 CFR 184.1697 covers nutrient supplementation of milk products and use in infant formula under the applicable conditions.

more_info.banned_in: JECFA records withdrawn specifications in 1984; no current EU or US food-colour listing was verified in 2026.
more_info.overview: Yellow 2G is an azo colour identified as C.I. Food Yellow 5 or Acid Yellow 17. Its food-colouring function is to supply yellow colour. JECFA records it as INS 107.
more_info.daily_intake: No ADI allocated (JECFA, 1979). The earlier temporary ADI is not the latest decision in the reviewed record.

names: Sunset Yellow FCF (Orange Yellow S, FD&C Yellow 6)

more_info.banned_in:
Approved in the EU.
Approved in the US.
EFSA replaced its temporary ADI with a revised ADI after reviewing additional data in 2014.
more_info.overview: Sunset Yellow FCF is a synthetic azo colour that gives foods an orange shade. Orange Yellow S and FD&C Yellow No. 6 are other names for the same colour. Food-grade material consists mainly of the dye's salts.
more_info.origin: Synthetic. Diazotised aminobenzenesulfonic acid is coupled with a hydroxynaphthalenesulfonic acid; the sodium salt is isolated and dried.
more_info.daily_intake: 4 mg/kg body weight per day (EFSA, 2014). This replaced EFSA's temporary 1 mg/kg body weight per day ADI from 2009.
more_info.side_effects:
At reported food uses and levels, EFSA's 2014 assessment found no safety concern and estimated exposures below its revised ADI. The limited evidence did not firmly link this individual dye with intolerance reactions or behavioural effects seen with mixtures.
High-dose rat feeding studies provided the toxicology basis for the ADI; these studies are not evidence of the same effects at ordinary food intakes.
more_info.uses: Permitted EU uses include confectionery, flavoured drinks, mustard, sauces and desserts, subject to limits. US batches of FD&C Yellow No. 6 require certification.

more_info.banned_in: JECFA records withdrawn specifications in 1984; no current EU or US food-colour listing was verified in 2026.
more_info.overview: Orange GGN is a monoazo colour historically identified as C.I. Food Orange 2. Its food-colouring role is to provide orange colour. It is chemically distinct from Sunset Yellow FCF.
more_info.side_effects:
Human effects at food-use levels were not established in the reviewed 1977 JECFA monograph.
Historical repeated-dose rat studies reported reduced liver vitamin A content at experimental doses. These old animal findings do not establish the same effect at human food-use levels.

more_info.banned_in:
Approved in the EU.
Approved in the US.
more_info.overview: Cochineal extract and carmine are red colours whose main pigment is carminic acid. Carmine is a metal complex made from that pigment. In foods these materials produce red shades.
more_info.origin: Animal-derived, specifically from dried female cochineal insects. Extraction releases carminic acid; reaction with aluminium forms carmine, sometimes with other metal ions.
more_info.daily_intake: 2.5 mg carminic acid/kg body weight per day (EFSA, 2015). This expresses the earlier 5 mg carmine/kg body weight ADI in terms of carminic acid content.
more_info.side_effects:
At food-use levels, allergic reactions to cochineal/carmine can occur; EFSA could not establish a threshold dose for allergy. Residual proteins were identified as a reason to improve purification.
The animal toxicity studies reviewed by EFSA did not justify lowering the existing ADI; this does not remove the separate allergy risk.
more_info.uses: Examples of permitted EU uses include certain red cheeses, fruit preparations, breakfast cereals and meat products. US use as cochineal extract or carmine is subject to food standards and good manufacturing practice.
more_info.dietary_restrictions: Not suitable for vegan or vegetarian diets because the colour is extracted from insects.
more_info.precautions: EFSA identified allergenic material in E120 and recommended manufacturing purification steps because no allergy threshold could be established.

more_info.banned_in:
Approved in the US.
FDA proposed revoking the orange-skin colour listing for industry abandonment in July 2026; the reviewed inventory still records that proposal.
more_info.overview: Citrus Red 2 is a dye used to colour orange skins. Its US food authorization is restricted to certain mature oranges. It is not an authorization to colour foods generally.
more_info.daily_intake: No safe intake determined; JECFA concluded that this colour should not be used as a food additive (1969).
more_info.side_effects:
Human effects at the restricted food-use level were not established in the reviewed JECFA monograph.
Animal studies reviewed in 1969 reported bladder changes and other toxicity at experimental doses, with inconsistent tumour findings. JECFA considered the unexplained results sufficient to reject food-additive use; this is not proof of cancer at the permitted orange-skin exposure.
more_info.uses: US authorization covers the skins of mature oranges not intended for processing, with a limit of 2 mg/kg calculated on the whole fruit.

more_info.banned_in: Approved in the EU.
more_info.overview: Carmoisine, also called azorubine, is a red azo food colour. Food-grade material consists mainly of colouring salts. It gives foods red to maroon shades.
more_info.origin: A synthetic azo dye, generally supplied as its sodium salt.
more_info.daily_intake: 4 mg/kg body weight per day (EFSA, 2009), retained in the 2015 exposure assessment.
more_info.side_effects:
At reported food uses, EFSA's refined 2015 exposure estimates were below the ADI. Limited evidence did not establish this individual colour as a cause of intolerance reactions or behavioural effects reported for mixtures.
A model using maximum permitted levels estimated that some high-consuming toddlers and children could exceed the ADI. This is an intake estimate, not an observed clinical effect.
more_info.uses: Examples include certain fruit preserves, flavoured processed cheeses and fish products, subject to EU food-category limits.

more_info.banned_in:
Banned in: United States.
Approved in the EU.
FDA cancelled food-use certificates for FD&C Red No. 2 in 1976.
more_info.overview: Amaranth is a synthetic red azo colour, also known as FD&C Red No. 2. It supplies red shades in foods where its use is permitted. The dye is chemically identified under C.I. Food Red 9.
more_info.origin: Synthetic. Naphthalenesulfonic acid compounds are coupled to form the dye, which is supplied mainly as the sodium salt.
more_info.daily_intake: 0.15 mg/kg body weight per day (EFSA, 2010). JECFA allocated 0–0.5 mg/kg body weight per day in 1984; the values differ.
more_info.side_effects:
At estimated food-use exposure, EFSA's 2013 refined assessment placed all assessed age groups below its ADI. This estimates intake and does not establish that no individual reactions occur.
Long-term and reproductive/developmental animal studies were used to derive EFSA's lower ADI in 2010; these are experimental hazard data rather than demonstrated effects at ordinary human food intakes.
more_info.uses: EU permitted uses include certain alcoholic drinks and fish roe other than sturgeon caviar, with limits. Use in US food is prohibited.

more_info.banned_in:
Approved in the EU.
EU permitted levels and categories were reduced from 2013; no US food-colour listing was verified in 2026.
more_info.overview: Ponceau 4R is a red azo food colour. It is also called Cochineal Red A or New Coccine. Its colour comes from a manufactured dye rather than the insect extract used for carmine.
more_info.origin: Synthetic. Diazotised naphthionic acid is coupled with a naphthol disulfonic acid, and the product is converted to its sodium salt.
more_info.daily_intake: 0.7 mg/kg body weight per day (EFSA, 2009). JECFA allocated 0–4 mg/kg body weight per day in 1983; the assessments differ.
more_info.side_effects:
At food-use levels, limited evidence did not firmly establish this dye alone as a cause of intolerance or behavioural effects. EFSA's refined 2015 exposure assessment found no ADI exceedance after EU limits were reduced.
Kidney changes in a long-term mouse study were used to derive the ADI. This animal finding is not evidence of the same effect at ordinary human food intakes.
more_info.uses: EU permitted categories include confectionery, flavoured drinks, desserts and certain sausages, subject to specific limits.

more_info.banned_in:
Banned in: United States.
FDA terminated its remaining food-use certificates for FD&C Red No. 4 in 1976.
more_info.overview: Ponceau SX, also called Scarlet GN or FD&C Red No. 4, is a red azo colour. It was formerly used in food, including maraschino cherries. Its historical E125 number does not confer current approval.

more_info.banned_in: JECFA records withdrawn specifications in 1984; no current EU or US food-colour listing was verified in 2026.
more_info.overview: Ponceau 6R is a red azo colour identified as C.I. Food Red 8. JECFA lists it under the former E126 designation. Its intended food function is colouring.
more_info.daily_intake: ADI decision postponed (JECFA, 1977); no ADI allocated in the 1974 assessment.
more_info.side_effects:
The 1974 JECFA monograph reported human sensitisation after oral intake. The small evidence base did not establish a reliable frequency or threshold at food-use levels.
The long-term animal studies were too small and incomplete to assess toxicity adequately, and reproductive data were missing. This assessment gap does not establish safety at high doses.

more_info.banned_in:
Approved in the EU.
Approved in the US.
FDA issued a revocation order in 2025; the food-use listing ends on 15 January 2027, so the US flag is retained for the 2026 check.
more_info.overview: Erythrosine is a red xanthene food dye also known as FD&C Red No. 3. EU food use is limited to particular cherry products. Its US listing has a future food-use termination date.
more_info.origin: Synthetic. Fluorescein, formed from resorcinol and phthalic anhydride, is iodinated to make the colour, which is supplied mainly as a sodium salt.
more_info.daily_intake: 0–0.1 mg/kg body weight per day (EFSA, 2011, retaining the earlier JECFA/SCF ADI).
more_info.side_effects:
At the food-use exposures estimated in 2011, EFSA found no safety concern and estimates were below the ADI.
High experimental exposure caused thyroid tumours in rats; EFSA considered the mechanism to have limited relevance to humans. FDA's 2025 revocation order applied the US statutory prohibition on colour additives that induce cancer in humans or animals.
more_info.uses: EU authorization covers cocktail and candied cherries, and Bigarreaux cherries in syrup or cocktails. US food use remains in its transition period.
